Regional identity and national unity

Regional aspirations arise when people seek greater recognition, economic development, representation or decision-making powers for a particular region or community.

Regional demands are not necessarily demands for separation from India. A movement may seek better development policies, a separate State within the Union, greater constitutional autonomy or, in some cases, independence.

These demands differ in their objectives and must be distinguished carefully.

DemandMeaningExample
Separate StateCreation of a new State within India.Mahagujarat Movement
Greater autonomyMore authority for a region within the Union.Regional autonomy demands in Punjab
Identity protectionRecognition of language, culture or local interests.Assam Movement
SecessionSeparation from India to form an independent political entity.Historical insurgency led by the Mizo National Front

Punjab: autonomy, militancy and the Punjab Accord

Following the linguistic reorganisation of Punjab in 1966, the Akali Dal continued to raise issues concerning State autonomy, religious identity and relations between the Union and the States.

The Anandpur Sahib Resolution of 1973 expressed important demands for greater regional autonomy and a redefinition of Centre–State relations. The resolution should be distinguished from later extremist demands for an independent Khalistan.

Punjab experienced a serious period of militancy and violence during the 1980s. In June 1984, the Union government conducted Operation Blue Star at the Golden Temple complex in Amritsar. The operation deeply affected Sikh sentiments and was followed by further violence.

Prime Minister Indira Gandhi was assassinated on 31 October 1984. Anti-Sikh violence then occurred in Delhi and several other places, causing extensive loss of life.

In July 1985, Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi and Akali leader Harchand Singh Longowal reached an agreement known as the Punjab Accord or Rajiv Gandhi–Longowal Accord. It addressed disputes including Chandigarh and other matters affecting Punjab and neighbouring States.

The agreement was an attempt to move from political conflict towards a negotiated settlement, although difficulties in implementation continued.

The Assam Movement, 1979–1985

In Assam, concerns developed over migration, electoral rolls, employment opportunities and the preservation of Assamese cultural and political identity.

The All Assam Students' Union (AASU) became a leading organisation in the Assam Movement of 1979–1985. The All Assam Gana Sangram Parishad (AAGSP) was another important organisation associated with the agitation.

The movement demanded identification of foreign nationals and changes to electoral arrangements. It also reflected concerns about economic development and local access to resources. The agitation involved extensive public mobilisation but also witnessed tragic episodes of violence.

The Assam Accord of 1985

The Assam Accord was signed on 15 August 1985 by representatives of the Union government, the Assam government, AASU and AAGSP.

Its provisions distinguished between people entering Assam during different periods. The important historical reference dates were 1 January 1966 and 24 March 1971. Those entering before 1 January 1966 were to be regularised; foreigners entering from 1 January 1966 to 24 March 1971 were to be detected, registered and excluded from electoral rolls for 10 years from detection; foreigners entering on or after 25 March 1971 were to be detected and expelled.

Leaders associated with the agitation subsequently formed the Asom Gana Parishad (AGP), which came to power in Assam in 1985.

The Accord was a political settlement, but its signing did not immediately resolve every dispute over migration and identity.

Mizoram: from insurgency to negotiated peace

In the Mizo Hills, dissatisfaction with the response to a severe famine in 1959 contributed to political mobilisation.

The Mizo National Front (MNF), led by Laldenga, subsequently pursued a demand for independence. Armed conflict developed in 1966 and continued for many years.

Negotiations eventually produced the Mizoram Peace Accord of 30 June 1986 between the Government of India and the MNF.

The agreement provided a basis for ending the insurgency and strengthening democratic political institutions. Mizoram became a full-fledged State on 20 February 1987.

The Mizoram Peace Accord was signed in 1986, but Mizoram attained Statehood in 1987. These are different events.

Autonomous Councils in the North-East

Not every demand for self-government requires creation of a separate State. Some tribal communities seek authority over local administration and customary affairs while remaining within an existing State.

The Sixth Schedule of the Constitution provides for autonomous district and regional councils in specified tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.

These councils have constitutionally specified powers concerning local administration and certain matters such as land and customary practices. Their powers are defined by the Constitution and applicable law; they are not equivalent to complete independence or unrestricted State sovereignty.

Jammu and Kashmir: autonomy and constitutional change

Jammu and Kashmir provides another example of regional aspirations involving identity, autonomy, political representation and relations with the Union.

Historically, Sheikh Abdullah and the National Conference were associated with demands for regional political representation. The former State had special constitutional arrangements under Article 370.

The region experienced serious political conflict and militancy from the late 1980s. Its constitutional arrangements later changed significantly in 2019.

Following constitutional measures concerning Article 370 and the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019, the former State was reorganised on 31 October 2019 into the Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir and the Union Territory of Ladakh. The former has a legislature under the statutory framework, while Ladakh does not have a legislature.

Therefore, a historical textbook description of Jammu and Kashmir as a State with its earlier Article 370 arrangements must not be treated as its unchanged constitutional position after 2019.

How has democratic accommodation worked?

Post-Independence India has used different constitutional and political responses to regional demands:

  • State reorganisation: Creating States to accommodate linguistic or regional identity, as with Gujarat in 1960.
  • Electoral competition: Allowing regional political parties to represent demands within legislatures.
  • Autonomous institutions: Providing specified powers to local and tribal institutions.
  • Negotiated settlements: Reaching agreements with movements, as in Assam in 1985 and Mizoram in 1986.

These responses have not eliminated every conflict. Their importance lies in providing constitutional and political means for addressing regional demands.

Connecting the political and social changes

The major developments studied in this subtopic are related. The weakening of Congress dominance in 1967 opened more space for opposition and regional parties. The Congress split of 1969 and victory of 1971 strengthened central political leadership. The Emergency of 1975–1977 exposed the danger of unchecked power, while the election of 1977 and constitutional reforms of 1978 restored and strengthened important democratic safeguards.

Meanwhile, movements such as Dalit Panthers, Chipko, SEWA, BKU and Narmada Bachao Andolan raised social and economic issues that were not adequately addressed through elections alone. Linguistic and regional movements demonstrated that democratic participation also includes demands for recognition, autonomy and institutional change.

Prelims focus

  • Anandpur Sahib Resolution: 1973; associated with the Akali Dal.
  • Punjab Accord: July 1985; Rajiv Gandhi and Harchand Singh Longowal.
  • Assam Movement: 1979–1985; AASU was a principal organisation.
  • Assam Accord: 15 August 1985.
  • Mizoram Peace Accord: 30 June 1986; Statehood: 20 February 1987.
  • Trap: Regional autonomy, formation of a separate State within India and secession are 3 different political demands.
